title: cross-run-history
description: The declaration of the harness-scoped logs under history_dir, and the whole of what decides which events reach them. One property per log, named for the file it declares, holding that log read as an array of parsed lines — a log being the gathering of every file of that name under the history directory: the root-level file, which holds every record written before records were written per segment and stays where it is, followed by one file per segment, a segment being a directory named for the writer that produced its records (a story's id for a run's records and the mandate record l5-plan writes for that story, or the moment of writing for a broad-mode inspection, which has no story to name), so that two branches never append to the same file and a merge between them has nothing to reconcile: its items.properties.event.enum enumerates the execution-history event kinds routed to that log, and its items.properties declare the fields a record there carries. Selection and record shape are therefore one file rather than a condition written into append_event, and adding a kind to a log is an edit here and nowhere else. The `event` property is the selection and is not itself projected: a record carries the other declared fields, so what routed it is read off the enum that named its kind rather than repeated on every line. A field the execution-history entry does not carry is omitted rather than written null, which is the rule execution-history.json already follows — and an entry that would leave a record missing a field the log's items.required names writes no record there at all, so a log's required list is the second half of its selection: a kind named in a log's enum reaches it only on the occurrences that carry what a line there must carry, which is how one kind can be named by two logs that record different facts about it. A record is a summary and never a copy: the per-run artifacts hold the detail, and a log that duplicated them would inherit their size and lose its queryability. The decision log is the one exception, and it is deliberate: a record there carries the decision's own words — its question, answer, source and rationale — because a reviewer checks a decision against the source it names after the run directory has been deleted, and once that directory is gone nothing else holds those words. It copies the decision and nothing else from the verdict. History is evidence, never state — nothing here is read back to make a routing decision. A run reads every file of every log at its start and reports, at its end, what a configured history_retention_days would drop; it rewrites nothing. The rewrite happens only through l5-prune, run by a person on the repository's default branch outside any run, so two runs never rewrite the same file and their branches merge without contending on the history. One further log is named here as RESERVED and is deliberately not declared above: adjudication-log.jsonl. This harness has no producer for it — adjudication is a level 4 concept it does not have — so it creates none, and naming it here rather than shipping an empty file is the whole of what it does about it. A later harness that acquires a producer declares its log as a property beside the ones above, and gets the projection with no change to orchestration — which is what inspection-log.jsonl, reserved here until this harness acquired the producer that writes it, now demonstrates rather than predicts. The per-log declarations are properties rather than a $defs block because the harness's own validator honors a deliberately small keyword subset and refuses a schema claiming a constraint it cannot check; a property named for its log carries the same declaration and stays checkable.

execution-log.jsonl.description: One record per point an execution reached, rather than one per execution that reached an outcome. Written to execution-log.jsonl under the segment of the history directory named for the writer that produced the record — .harness/history/<story-id>/ for a record with a story to name, and a segment named for the moment it was written for one without — one JSON object per line, appended as the point is reached rather than assembled as a terminal summary. A run that paused for capacity, was resumed and then completed therefore leaves three lines in that order, so a resumed execution is distinguishable in the record from an uninterrupted one — which is the whole reason a pause and a resume are recorded here at all: a pause carries its own exit code precisely so a caller can tell it from completion and from escalation, and an execution that reached one and left no line was indistinguishable in this log from one that never started.

event.description: The execution-history event kinds routed to this log. This enum is the selection and nothing else decides it: an entry whose kind appears here is projected into this log, and an entry whose kind appears in no log's enum is projected nowhere. The property is not projected into a record: it declares which kinds arrive here, not a field a line carries.

story_id.description: The story this execution ran, derived from the run directory's own name.

status.description: The point the execution reached, derived from the event kind that produced the record rather than threaded through the coordinator to serve this projection. Two of these values do not end an execution: capacity-paused says the run stopped to wait, and resumed says it continued, so a line carrying either is a point rather than an outcome.

retry_count.description: How many retries the execution took, counted from the retry decisions already present in the run's own execution history, which append_event has loaded to number the entry it is appending.

verifier_outcome.description: The verifier's verdict, when the entry that produced this record carried one. Absent otherwise.

timestamp.description: When the outcome occurred, in the same YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS form events.log and execution-history.json use. It is what history_retention_days is compared against.

inspection-log.jsonl.description: One record per inspection, in either mode: the narrow one a run makes of what its story changed, and the broad one an l5-inspect invocation makes of a part of the tree. Written to inspection-log.jsonl under the segment of the history directory named for the writer that produced the record — .harness/history/<story-id>/ for a record with a story to name, and a segment named for the moment it was written for one without — one JSON object per line, appended as the inspection ends. It exists because the run directory is gitignored and reaches no clone: an inspection reporting only into that run's events.log would leave no evidence in the repository that any inspection had ever run, and a broad-mode inspection has no run directory to report into at all. A record is a summary and never a copy — what was found, filed and dropped is here as three counts, and which finding went which way is in the run's own events.log and in the outbox entries the inspection wrote. Both modes carry the same fields, so one read of one file answers what inspection has cost across both without walking any run directory. The inspection is a total function that may not block, delay or refuse a run, so a record here is also what a configuration it could not obey is named in: an inspection that was not made because the file cap was unusable leaves a line saying so with its counts at zero, because naming the problem is the only thing a function that cannot refuse can do about it. Beside the inspection records sits a second kind of record about one of them: the accounting a run writes after the verdict, once per attempt that routed findings to the story. An inspection made ahead of the judging stage routes its findings about the story's own change to that stage rather than filing them, and the inspection's own record says how many were routed; the accounting record says what became of them — how many the verdict acted on, and how many of the rest were held for the run's completion. It carries no cost_usd and no invocations, because it made no invocation, and its filed and dropped counts are zero, because it files nothing. It is what lets a reader of this log tell a finding the story answered from one the verifier passed over, which the inspection record alone cannot say because it is written before the verdict exists. A third kind of record is the filing a run makes at completion: nothing an inspection finds during a run reaches the queue until the run completes, so the final attempt's held findings and the remainder its verdict left are filed then, once, and this record says how many were filed and dropped. It carries filed and dropped and a story_id, and none of the fields the other two kinds carry, which is how it is told apart. It is written for a completed run that filed or dropped something, and also for a run whose filing could not run, where it carries filed and dropped at zero and the run's own events.log names the failure. A fourth kind is what the run abandoned: a verdict that asks for a finding to be corrected or repaired and meets an allowance the run has already spent leaves that finding with no pass to run for it, and the record says how many. It carries abandoned and none of the fields the other three carry, which is how it is told apart, and it is written only by a run that abandoned something — the event it is projected from fires only where an allowance was spent, so a run that abandoned nothing leaves no line of this kind. It is the whole of what makes an abandonment durable: the findings themselves are named in the run's own events.log, which is gitignored and is deleted when the story is cleaned up. An abandoned finding is still left by the verdict rather than acted on by it, so the accounting record for that attempt carries it in the remainder and the filing record says what became of it.

event.description: The execution-history event kinds routed to this log, on the terms the execution log's own event property states: this enum is the selection, and the property is not projected into a record. It names the inspection's own kind, the accounting's and the completion filing's. The accounting's and the filing's are named by no other log's enum; the inspection's own kind is also named by duration-log.jsonl, which records how long the inspection took where this log records what it found, and only the occurrences of it that carry a duration — an inspection that made its invocation — reach that log, by the required-field rule the top-level description states. None of the three reaches execution-log.jsonl, mandate-log.jsonl or retry-log.jsonl. It also names the two kinds a run writes when a pass allowance is spent, which are one further kind of record here: what the run abandoned. Because the kind is not projected, which of the four a line is has to be read off its fields: an accounting record carries `routed` and `acted_on`, an inspection record carries `mode`, `invocations` and `dedupe_ran`, a filing record carries `filed` and `dropped` and none of those, and an abandonment record carries `abandoned` and none of the others.

story_id.description: The story whose completed run made this inspection, derived from the run directory's own name. Absent for a broad-mode inspection, which is not made by a run and has no story to name: it is outside this log's required list for that reason alone, and a narrow-mode record carries it exactly as it always has.

mode.description: Which inspection made this record. 'broad' is an l5-inspect invocation over a part of the tree; 'narrow' is the inspection a completed run makes of what its story changed. It is here because the two modes run at different frequencies against different scopes — narrow mode fires on every completed story, several times a day — so a corpus that could not separate them could not be used to tune either.

cost_usd.description: What this inspection's invocations reported spending, in US dollars, summed across them. Carried and never computed: it is the figure the runner's own result reported, and nothing re-derives it by reading an agent log back. Absent where no invocation reported a cost, rather than written as zero — a zero would be indistinguishable from an inspection that genuinely cost nothing and would corrupt any average taken over this log later.

scope_files.description: How many files this inspection had in scope, summed across its invocations. What a cost means depends on how much was read, so the two are recorded together.

invocations.description: How many agent invocations the recorded cost covers. Broad mode makes one per scope and narrow mode makes one, and either makes a second for a scope whose first produced no findings artifact — so a cost read without this could not be read as a per-invocation figure, and a count higher than the scopes inspected is how a reader knows a retry happened. The ceiling an invocation runs under is per invocation, so a second one is handed its own allowance rather than what the first left: the cost here is their sum and can exceed one allowance. Zero is an inspection that invoked nothing at all.

timestamp.description: When the inspection ended, in the same YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS form events.log and execution-history.json use. It is what history_retention_days is compared against.

findings.description: How many findings the invocation produced. Present even where it is zero: an inspection that found nothing is an answer, and a line whose counts are all zero is how an inspection that was not made at all is distinguished from one nobody ran.

filed.description: How many of those findings reached the outbox as briefs. On an inspection made ahead of the judging stage and on the accounting after its verdict it is zero, because nothing an inspection finds during a run reaches the queue until the run completes; on the filing record written at completion it is how many of the final attempt's held findings and remainder were filed.

dropped.description: How many were dropped, for every reason together. Which way each went is not summarised here: it is in the run's own events.log, where each reason is named with how many went that way. Zero on an accounting record, which files nothing and so drops nothing; on the filing record it is how many of what was filed at completion were dropped.

routed.description: On an accounting record: how many findings the pre-stage inspection routed to the story on the attempt being accounted — the findings about the story's own change, handed to the stage that judges it rather than filed. Absent on an inspection record, whose `findings` count includes them. Carried here because the inspection record is written before the verdict exists and can say only that they were routed; this record is written after it and says what became of them.

acted_on.description: On an accounting record: how many of the routed findings the verdict acted on, decided by the verdict naming the finding's slug in the location of a blocking issue, a correctable finding or a repairable finding — never by file. The routed findings not counted here are the remainder, held for the run's completion and filed then by the filing record, if that attempt was the final one. Present even where it is zero, because none acted on is an answer, and absent on an inspection record. An accounting record carries no cost_usd, no invocations and no dedupe_ran: it made no invocation and asked no query.

abandoned.description: On an abandonment record: how many findings a spent pass allowance abandoned. The verdict asked for them to be corrected or repaired, the run had no allowance left to run that pass with, and no pass was run for them — so the finding went nowhere unless something recorded it, which is what this is. It is present on that record alone and absent on the three kinds beside it, so a reader tells them apart by the fields each carries rather than by prose, the kind itself not being projected. Which findings they were is not summarised here: they are named in the run's own events.log. It counts every finding the verdict named for the pass, which the verifier may raise itself as readily as the inspection may route one to the story, and the two are told apart by what else is recorded for each. A routed finding is left by the verdict rather than acted on by it, so it is accounted for individually in the run's completion report, and it is not lost to the backlog either: the filing at the run's completion sends it on through the same call every other producer files through, and the queue's own duplicate detection is what stops a later run that meets the same spent allowance filing it again. A finding the verifier raised itself was never routed, and since story-221 it is accounted all the same: the attempt's accounting records it under a key of its own while the run leaves it, the completion report names it by that key, and the filing at the run's completion sends it to the backlog as a brief built from the classification the verifier gave it, or drops it with its reason named in the run's completion line and in the report where it carries none.

dedupe_ran.description: Whether this inspection's filed query answered for every scope it covered. False is an inspection made without dedupe: the findings were filed anyway, because a query that could not answer costs dedupe and costs nothing else, so what a false records is that this inspection may have refiled what is already in the tracker. It is a statement about the filed query alone. The local outbox queue is read as a second dedupe source and reading it successfully does not make dedupe complete — it holds only what this machine filed, so a brief filed from another checkout, another developer or the tracker's own interface is invisible to it, and the tracker's answer is the only tier that can see one. An absent tracker answer is therefore not an empty one: nothing filed and nothing known look identical in an item list, and this field is what separates them once the inspection is over and the run directory it reported into is gone. It is written by both modes and on every line, including one where the query did answer, because a boolean has a false to say and absence would then mean either that or a line written before this field existed. An inspection that made no invocation at all — the file cap unusable, nothing the story changed in an inspected scope, an inspection that could not run — records false, because no query answered for it. Which scope's query failed and why is not summarised here: it is in the run's own events.log for a narrow-mode inspection, where a failed dedupe gets a line of its own naming the scope and the reason, and in what l5-inspect printed for a broad one.

inspection_made.description: Whether an invocation of this inspection produced a findings report to read. False is an inspection that could not be made: an invocation produced no findings artifact, was made once more because a reviewer's process can die before it writes anything, and produced none again — so nothing is known about what that reviewer would have said. What it records is the distinction this log could not previously be asked for: such an inspection reported zero findings, which is exactly what an inspection that looked and found nothing reports, so the two were one line in this log and the findings the dead one would have raised were lost with no signal. A false does not mean the change is clean and does not mean the inspection found nothing; it means nothing looked. It is not the number of findings by another name, either: an invocation that wrote a well-formed report carrying an empty findings array is a real answer and records true with `findings` zero, because the trigger for the retry and for this field is the absence of the file and never what the file said. It is written by both modes and on every record, including one where the inspection was made, because a boolean has a false to say and absence would then mean either that or a line written before this field existed — the treatment `dedupe_ran` beside it already gets, and for the same reason: a field written only when false is a field nobody can query for the runs where it was true. An inspection that made no invocation at all — the file cap unusable, nothing the story changed in an inspected scope, an inspection that could not run — records false, because nothing produced a report for it either. Which invocations produced nothing, and what each failed at, is not summarised here: it is in the run's own events.log, where the line naming the drop names both invocations, and in what l5-inspect printed for a broad-mode one. In broad mode, which makes one invocation per scope, a false is at least one scope that produced no report after its retry.

mandate-log.jsonl.description: One record per mandate conferred: the harness-scoped record of an authorizing act, written by the process that observed it rather than by a run. Written to mandate-log.jsonl under the segment of the history directory named for the writer that produced the record — .harness/history/<story-id>/ for a record with a story to name, and a segment named for the moment it was written for one without — one JSON object per line, appended as the act is observed. It is the only declared log with no producer inside a run — no execution-history entry the coordinator appends carries this kind, so nothing a run does reaches it, and what does reach it is a caller outside a run using the same per-log append with an explicit history directory. That is the whole of what makes the conferring record a schema entry rather than a condition in orchestration: adding the kind here is what routes it, exactly as it is for the two logs beside this one. A record is a summary and never a copy: the block it records lives in the artifact it was appended to, and this line is what outlives the working tree that artifact was written in.

event.description: The event kinds routed to this log, on the terms the execution log's own event property states: this enum is the selection, and the property is not projected into a record.

story_id.description: The work item the mandate was conferred on.

timestamp.description: When the authorizing act was observed, in the same YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS form events.log and execution-history.json use. It is what history_retention_days is compared against, and it is the conferred_at the block itself carries.

conferred_by.description: The identity the act was observed from, as the block records it.

source_kind.description: The kind of source the block names, so a reader can tell what a run's resolution would have terminated at without opening the artifact.

recorded_by.description: The harness process that observed the act and wrote the block. Absent when the entry carried none.

discarded_session_block.description: Whether this conferral discarded a mandate block the planning session had written into the artifact. The observing process refuses such a block rather than trusting it, and the developer it asks is shown that the block is there and that approving discards it, so a true here records an approval given with that in front of them and a false records a conferral onto an artifact that carried none. It is written on every conferral rather than only on the true case, because a boolean has a false to say and absence would then mean either that or a record written before this field existed. A rejection writes no record at all — nothing was conferred, and this log holds conferrals — so a plan the developer declined leaves no line here, and that absence is the mechanism working rather than a gap in it.

retry-log.jsonl.description: One record per retry a story's execution took. Written to retry-log.jsonl under the segment of the history directory named for the writer that produced the record — .harness/history/<story-id>/ for a record with a story to name, and a segment named for the moment it was written for one without — one JSON object per line, appended as the retry is routed.

event.description: The execution-history event kinds routed to this log, on the terms the execution log's own event property states: this enum is the selection, and the property is not projected into a record.

story_id.description: The story whose execution took this retry, derived from the run directory's own name.

timestamp.description: When the retry was routed, in the same YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS form events.log and execution-history.json use. It is what history_retention_days is compared against.

stage.description: The stage the entry belongs to. Absent when the entry carried none.

retry_decision.description: The routing decision the entry recorded. Absent when the entry carried none.

retry_category.description: The retry category the verifier reported, as the workflow's retry_routing table declares it. Absent on a retry that carries no category.

retry_stage.description: The stage the retry was routed to. On a self-routed entry it names the entry's own stage, because a self-route has no destination other than itself.

duration-log.jsonl.description: One record per timed operation per occurrence: how long each long step of a run took, kept so a later run can say, when it announces that step, how long it is expected to take. Written to duration-log.jsonl under the segment of the history directory named for the story whose run made the record, one JSON object per line, appended as each operation completes. The operations are every stage, the clean-clone check, the suite run a stage declares, the revert check's whole-suite fallthrough, the suite census and the inspection — recorded under one name whichever position the loaded workflow runs it in, before its declaring stage or after the story completes, because each run makes one or the other and the invocation timed is the same; the revert check's nomination selector, the outbox sweep and the suite-turn wait are not timed and leave no record here, because each announces a bound rather than a guess. A record is read by two things, and both read it off the startup read a run already makes of the whole history rather than reading the directory again. The first establishes, per operation, the median of a bounded window of the most recent observations ordered by this record's timestamp, and only where enough exist — otherwise the step announces exactly what it announced before this log existed. The second derives what the whole story takes, which adding the per-operation figures up would answer wrongly, because they cover one pass through the work and some runs go round again: the records carrying one story_id are summed into one total for that story, a story counts only where the execution log records it as completed, and a story is sent back when its records hold more than one for the loaded workflow's first stage. A starting run says the median total of the recent stories that went straight through, the median of those that were sent back, and the share that were, and says that the figures are working time and exclude waiting for the machine — announced only where both groups hold enough stories, and otherwise not announced at all. Both figures are a report to a person and never a bound: no timeout reads either, no check compares against either, and an operation or a story that runs past one is an operation or a story, running. A record whose duration_seconds is not a number, or whose timestamp cannot be read, is not an observation and stops nothing. The enum below names completion kinds that other logs' enums also name — inspection-completed reaches inspection-log.jsonl as well, and verification-failed reaches retry-log.jsonl — and the required list is what keeps an occurrence that was not timed out of here: a revert check decided by its nomination selector completes with no duration and no operation and so writes no line in this log.

event.description: The execution-history event kinds routed to this log, on the terms the execution log's own event property states: this enum is the selection, and the property is not projected into a record. They are the kinds that complete a timed operation — a stage's completion is stage-completed for every stage but the verifying one, whose completion is verification-passed or verification-failed — and a kind here may also be named by another log that records a different fact about the same completion.

story_id.description: The story whose run made this observation, derived from the run directory's own name.

operation.description: Which operation the observation is of: a stage's own name for a stage, and a fixed name for each check and the inspection, exactly as the execution-history entry's operation field spells it. It is the key an estimate is read under.

duration_seconds.description: How long that occurrence took, in seconds, as the completing entry carried it. A line whose value is not a number is kept and is not an observation.

timestamp.description: When the operation completed, in the same YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS form events.log and execution-history.json use. It is what orders the observations an estimate is read from, most recent first, and what history_retention_days is compared against.

decision-log.jsonl.description: One record per decision a run made and one per decision it rejected: the ledger of the choices a run made where its approved plan was silent and an existing source settled the question. Written to decision-log.jsonl under the segment of the history directory named for the story whose run made the record, one JSON object per line, appended as each decision is made and as each rejection is judged. A decision is recorded where the repair pass carrying it is routed, and nowhere else: a decision whose pass a spent allowance refused, one a correction pass deferred, and one the coordinator refused for naming no source record nothing here, and a run resumed inside the pass records nothing twice, because a resume re-enters at the saved stage without routing again. A rejection is a record of its own — the verification the pass returned to rejected the decision, and the line says which decision and why — and the decision's own record is never rewritten, so the log is append-only in the sense the book's decision ledger is. The two are told apart by their fields, since the kind is not projected: a decision record carries answer, source, rationale, confidence and blast_radius, and a rejection record carries rejection. Unlike the logs beside it, a record here carries the decision's own words rather than counts — the exception the top-level description states, because once the run directory is deleted nothing else holds them and a reviewer reading the decisions after the run is the reason the log exists. Nothing routes on any field here, confidence and blast_radius included: they are recorded so a reviewer can read the risky decisions first.

event.description: The execution-history event kinds routed to this log, on the terms the execution log's own event property states: this enum is the selection, and the property is not projected into a record. Neither kind is named by any other log, so neither reaches another log by accident, and the decision-refused kind is named by none, so a refused decision reaches no log at all.

story_id.description: The story whose run made or rejected the decision, derived from the run directory's own name.

timestamp.description: When the decision was recorded or the rejection judged, in the same YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS form events.log and execution-history.json use. It is what history_retention_days is compared against.

stage.description: The stage that made the decision, or that rejected it: the verifying stage whose verdict carried it.

finding.description: The location of the repairable finding the decision was made for, as the verdict recorded it — the file and the slug a reviewer opens it by.

question.description: The question the decision answers: the choice its fix requires that the approved plan does not make. On a rejection record it names the decision rejected.

answer.description: The answer chosen. On a decision record alone.

source.description: The existing source that settles the question — a repository standard, a configured architecture document, or the place in the codebase that already solves the same problem — so a reviewer can open it and check the decision against it. On a decision record alone.

rationale.description: Why this answer rather than another. On a decision record alone.

confidence.description: How sure the run was that the source settles the question, in the vocabulary a brief's confidence uses. On a decision record alone, and read by nothing that routes.

blast_radius.description: How costly a wrong answer would be to undo. On a decision record alone, and read by nothing that routes.

rejection.description: Why the verification the decided repair returned to rejected the decision, in its own words. On a rejection record alone.
